source_text: Καὶ ἐγένετο οὕτως. Ἀρκοῦσα αὕτη ἡ ἐπαγωγὴ πρὸς τὸ δεῖξαι εἰς ἔργον ἐλθοῦσαν τοῦ δημιουργοῦ τὴν φωνήν. Πρόσκειται δὲ ἐν πολλοῖς τῶν ἀντιγράφων, Καὶ συνήχθη τὸ ὕδωρ τὸ ὑποκάτω τοῦ οὐρανοῦ εἰς τὰς συναγωγὰς αὐτῶν, καὶ ὤφθη ἡ ξηρά· ἅπερ οὔτε τινὲς τῶν λοιπῶν ἐκδεδώκασιν ἑρμη νέων, οὔτε ἡ χρῆσις τῶν Ἑβραίων ἔχουσα φαίνεται. Καὶ γὰρ τῷ ὄντι παρέλκει μετὰ τὴν μαρτυρίαν τοῦ, ὅτι Ἐγένετο οὕτως, ἡ τῶν αὐτῶν πάλιν ἐπεκδιήγησις. Τὰ τοίνυν ἀκριβῆ τῶν ἀντιγράφων ὠβέλισται· ὁ δὲ ὀβελὸς, ἀθετήσεως σύμβο λον. Καὶ ἐκάλεσεν ὁ Θεὸς τὴν ξηρὰν, γῆν, καὶ τὰ συστήματα τῶν ὑδάτων ἐκάλεσε θαλάσσας. Διὰ τί καὶ ἐν τοῖς κατόπιν εἴρηται, Συναχθήτω τὰ ὕδατα εἰς συναγωγὴν μίαν, καὶ ὀφθήτω ἡ ξηρὰ, ἀλλ' οὐχὶ γέγραπται, καὶ ὀφθήτω ἡ γῆ; καὶ ἐνταῦθα πάλιν, Ὤφθη ξηρὰ, καὶ ἐκάλεσεν ὁ Θεὸς τὴν ξηρὰν, γῆν; Ὅτι ἡ μὲν ξηρὰ τὸ ἰδίωμά ἐστι, τὸ οἱονεὶ χαρακτηριστικὸν τῆς φύσεως τοῦ ὑποκειμένου, ἡ δὲ γῆ προσηγορία τίς ἐστι ψιλὴ τοῦ πράγματος. Ὡς γὰρ τὸ λογικὸν ἴδιόν ἐστι τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ἡ δὲ ἄνθρωπος φωνὴ σημαντική ἐστι τοῦ ζῴου ᾧ ὑπάρχει τὸ ἴδιον· οὕτω καὶ τὸ ξηρὸν ἴδιόν ἐστι τῆς γῆς καὶ ἐξαίρετον. Ὧ τοίνυν ἰδίως ὑπάρχει τὸ ξηρὸν, τοῦτο ἐπικέκληται γῆ· ὥσπερ ᾧ ἰδίως πρόσεστι τὸ χρεμετιστικὸν, τοῦτο ἐπικέκληται ἵππος. Οὐ μόνον δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἔστι τοῦτο, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν ἄλλων στοιχείων ἕκαστον ἰδιάζουσαν καὶ ἀποκεκληρωμένην ἔχει ποιότητα, δι' ἧς τῶν τε λοιπῶν ἀποκρίνεται, καὶ αὐτὸ ἕκαστον ὁποῖόν ἐστιν ἐπιγινώσκεται. Τὸ μὲν ὕδωρ ἰδίαν ποιότητα τὴν ψυχρότητα ἔχει· ὁ δὲ ἀὴρ τὴν ὑγρότητα· τὸ δὲ πῦρ τὴν θερμότητα. Ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν, ὡς πρῶτα στοιχεῖα τῶν συνθέτων κατὰ τὸν εἰρημένον τρόπον τῷ λογισμῷ θεωρεῖται, τὰ δὲ ἤδη ἐν σώματι κατατεταγμένα καὶ ὑποπίπτοντα τῇ αἰσθήσει, συνεζευγμένας ἔχει τὰς ποιότητας. Καὶ οὐδὲν ἀπολελυμένως ἐστὶ μοναχὸν οὐδὲ ἁπλοῦν καὶ εἰλικρινὲς τῶν ὁρωμένων καὶ αἰσθητῶν· ἀλλ' ἡ μὲν γῆ ξηρὰ καὶ ψυχρὰ, τὸ δὲ ὕδωρ ὑγρὸν καὶ ψυχρὸν, ὁ δὲ ἀὴρ θερμὸς καὶ ὑγρὸς, τὸ δὲ πῦρ θερμὸν καὶ ξηρόν, Οὕτω γὰρ, διὰ τῆς συζύγου ποιότητος, ἡ δύναμις προέρχεται τοῦ ἀναμιχθῆναι ἑκάστῳ πρὸς ἕκαστον· τῷ τε γὰρ γείτονι στοιχείῳ διὰ τῆς κοινῆς ποιότητος ἕκαστον ἀνακίρναται, καὶ διὰ τῆς πρὸς τὸ σύνεγγυς κοινωνίας τῷ ἀντικειμένῳ συνάπτεται. Οἷον, ἡ γῆ, ξηρὰ οὖσα καὶ ψυχρὰ, ἑνοῦται μὲν τῷ ὕδατι κατὰ τὴν συγγένειαν τῆς ψυχρότητος, ἑνοῦται δὲ διὰ τοῦ ὕδατος τῷ ἀέρι· ἐπειδὴ μέσον ἀμφοτέρων τεταγμένον τὸ ὕδωρ, οἱονεὶ χειρῶν δύο ἐπιβολῇ ἑκατέρᾳ ποιότητι τῶν παρακειμένων ἐφάπτεται, τῇ μὲν ψυχρότητι τῆς γῆς, τῇ ὑγρότητι δὲ τοῦ ἀέρος. Πάλιν ὁ ἀὴρ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ μεσιτείᾳ διαλλακτὴς γίνεται τῆς μαχομένης φύσεως ὕδατος καὶ πυρὸς, τῷ ὕδατι μὲν διὰ τῆς ὑγρότητος, τῷ πυρὶ δὲ διὰ τοῦ θερμοῦ συμπλεκόμενος. Τὸ δὲ πῦρ θερμὸν καὶ ξηρὸν ὑπάρχον τὴν φύσιν, τῷ μὲν θερμῷ πρὸς τὸν ἀέρα συνδεῖται, τῷ ξηρῷ δὲ πάλιν πρὸς τὴν κοινωνίαν τῆς γῆς ἐπανέρχεται.
thought_title: The dry land's proper quality and the naming of earth
orientation: Basil is explaining why Genesis says 'the dry land appeared' and then 'God called the dry land earth,' arguing that dryness is the defining quality of earth, and he extends this to the four elements and their paired qualities.
pass_a_gloss: And it became so. This addition is sufficient to show that the voice of the Creator came into deed. And it is added in many of the copies, 'And the water under heaven was gathered into their gatherings, and the dry land appeared'; which things neither some of the remaining interpreters have published, nor does the usage of the Hebrews appear to have. For indeed truly after the testimony that 'It became so,' the re-explanation of the same things is superfluous. The accurate copies therefore have been marked with an obelus; and the obelus is a sign of rejection. And God called the dry land earth, and the gatherings of the waters he called seas. Why also in the earlier passages it was said, 'Let the waters be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear,' but it has not been written, 'and let the earth appear'? And here again, 'The dry land appeared, and God called the dry land earth'? Because the dry is the peculiar property, the as it were characteristic of the nature of the underlying thing, but earth is a bare appellation of the thing. For as the rational is proper to man, and the word 'man' is significant of the animal to which the property belongs; so also the dry is proper to earth and exceptional. That therefore to which the dry belongs properly, this has been called earth; just as that to which the neighing properly belongs, this has been called horse. And not only in the case of earth is this so, but also each of the other elements has a peculiar and allotted quality, through which it is distinguished from the rest, and each itself is recognized as what sort it is. Water has as its own quality coldness; air has moisture; fire has heat. But these things, as first elements of composite things according to the manner stated, are contemplated by reason, but the things already arranged in body and falling under sense have the qualities joined together. And nothing of the visible and sensible things is absolutely solitary nor simple and pure; but earth is dry and cold, water is moist and cold, air is hot and moist, fire is hot and dry. For thus, through the paired quality, the power proceeds for each to be mixed with each; for each is blended with the neighboring element through the common quality, and through the fellowship with the near one it is joined to the opposite. For example, earth, being dry and cold, is united to water according to the kinship of coldness, and is united through water to air; since water, placed in the middle of both, as it were by the application of two hands touches each quality of the adjacent elements, by coldness to earth, by moisture to air. Again air by its own mediation becomes reconciler of the warring nature of water and fire, being intertwined with water through moisture, and with fire through heat. And fire, being hot and dry in nature, is bound to air by the hot, and by the dry again returns to fellowship with earth.

lemmas.gloss: have been marked with an obelus

choices.why: ἐπαγωγή here means the appended clause 'And it became so,' not an induction or argument; 'addition' captures the textual-critical sense.

choices.english: have been marked with an obelus
choices.why: Basil is using the technical Alexandrian text-critical term for marking spurious lines; keeping the technical term 'obelus' preserves his scholarly register.

choices.term: τὸ ἰδίωμά ἐστι, τὸ οἱονεὶ χαρακτηριστικὸν τῆς φύσεως
choices.english: is the peculiar property, the as it were characteristic of the nature
choices.why: ἰδίωμα is a technical philosophical term for a defining property; 'peculiar property' keeps the technical sense, and 'as it were' renders οἱονεί.

choices.term: προσηγορία τίς ἐστι ψιλὴ τοῦ πράγματος
choices.english: is a bare appellation of the thing
choices.why: ψιλή means 'bare' or 'mere,' contrasting a mere name with a defining property; 'bare appellation' preserves the philosophical contrast.
rejected: is a simple name of the thing
is a mere designation of the thing

choices.english: has a peculiar and allotted quality
choices.why: ἀποκληρόω means to assign by lot; 'allotted' conveys the sense of a fixed, divinely assigned quality proper to each element.

choices.english: becomes reconciler of the warring nature
choices.why: διαλλακτής is an agent noun meaning one who reconciles; 'reconciler' preserves the active role of air in mediating between water and fire.
rejected: becomes mediator of the conflicting nature
becomes arbitrator of the opposing nature

pass_b_english: “And it became so.” This sequel is sufficient to show that the Creator’s voice came to fulfillment in deed. But in many copies there is added: “And the water under heaven was gathered into its gatherings, and the dry land appeared”—which neither some of the other translators have published, nor does the usage of the Hebrews appear to contain. For in truth, after the testimony that “It became so,” the further detailed narration of the same things is redundant. In the accurate copies, then, these words have been marked with an obelus; and the obelus is a sign of rejection. “And God called the dry land earth, and the gatherings of the waters he called seas” (Genesis 1:10). Why is it that earlier it says, “Let the waters be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear” (Genesis 1:9), but it is not written, “and let the earth appear”? And here again, “The dry land appeared, and God called the dry land earth”? Because “dry” is the peculiar property, the as it were characteristic of the nature of the underlying thing, while “earth” is a bare appellation of the thing. For just as rationality is the peculiar property of a human being, while the word “human being” signifies the animal in which that property resides, so also dryness is the peculiar and exceptional property of earth. That, then, which properly possesses dryness is called earth—just as that which properly possesses the neighing property is called a horse. And this is true not only of earth, but each of the other elements also has a peculiar and allotted quality, by which it is distinguished from the rest and by which each is recognized for what it is. Water has coldness as its own quality; air has moisture; fire has heat. But these, as the first elements of composite things, are contemplated by reason in the manner described; the things already arranged in body and falling under sense perception have their qualities joined together. And nothing among visible and perceptible things is absolutely single or simple and pure; rather, earth is dry and cold, water is moist and cold, air is hot and moist, fire is hot and dry. For in this way, through the paired quality, the power of each to mix with each comes forth. Each element is blended with its neighboring element through their common quality, and through its fellowship with what is near it is joined to its opposite. For example, earth, being dry and cold, is united to water through the kinship of coldness, and through water it is united to air; since water is placed in the middle between both, as if by the laying on of two hands it touches each of the adjacent elements with each quality—earth with its coldness, air with its moisture. Again, air by its own mediation becomes reconciler of the warring nature of water and fire, being intertwined with water through moisture and with fire through heat. And fire, being hot and dry in nature, is bound to air by its heat, and by its dryness it returns again to fellowship with earth.
notes: The source text has a line break in the middle of ἑρμη νέων (interpreters) and σύμβο λον (sign), likely due to manuscript line division; the words are complete.

problems.why: ἐπαγωγὴ means 'conclusion/sequel,' not 'addition'; it refers to the phrase just quoted.
problems.ruling: ἐπαγωγὴ means 'conclusion/sequel,' not 'addition'; it refers to the quoted phrase, not an insertion.

fixed: Changed 'This addition' to 'This sequel' because ἐπαγωγὴ means 'conclusion/sequel,' referring to the phrase just quoted, not an addition.

last_rejected.why: ἐπαγωγὴ means 'addition' or 'appendix,' not 'sequel'; it refers to the added phrase in manuscripts.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπαγωγὴ can mean 'addition' or 'sequel'; both fit context of added text. Within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: which neither some of the other translators have published
last_rejected.source_quote: ἅπερ οὔτε τινὲς τῶν λοιπῶν ἐκδεδώκασιν ἑρμηνέων
last_rejected.why: οὔτε...οὔτε construction means 'neither...nor,' but 'some' with 'neither' creates a logical problem; the Greek says 'neither have some of the other translators published, nor does the Hebrew usage appear to contain them.'
last_rejected.fix: which neither have some of the other translators published
last_rejected.ruling: τινὲς with οὔτε is normal Greek 'neither some...nor'; no logical problem. Rendering is accurate.

last_rejected.quote: the further detailed narration of the same things is redundant
last_rejected.why: παρέλκει means 'is superfluous' or 'is dragged in unnecessarily,' not 'is redundant'; the phrase misrepresents Basil's point about textual criticism.
last_rejected.fix: the further detailed narration of the same things is superfluous
last_rejected.ruling: παρέλκει means 'is superfluous/redundant'; both overlap in meaning. Mere preference, not error.

last_rejected.source_quote: ἴδιόν ἐστι τῆς γῆς καὶ ἐξαίρετον
last_rejected.why: ἐξαίρετον means 'distinctive' or 'particular,' not 'exceptional'; 'exceptional' suggests superiority rather than distinguishing characteristic.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐξαίρετον can mean 'exceptional' or 'distinctive'; both convey distinguishing quality. Normal range.

last_rejected.quote: the things already arranged in body
last_rejected.source_quote: τὰ δὲ ἤδη ἐν σώματι κατατεταγμένα
last_rejected.why: ἐν σώματι means 'in a body' or 'embodied,' not 'in body'; this refers to composite physical things, not things arranged inside a body.
last_rejected.fix: the things already embodied and falling under sense perception
last_rejected.ruling: ἐν σώματι 'in body' vs 'in a body' is minor; context of composite bodies is preserved. Not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: absolutely single or simple and pure
last_rejected.why: μοναχὸν means 'solitary' or 'isolated,' not 'single' in the sense of simple; the phrase means nothing exists in isolation, simply and purely.
last_rejected.fix: nothing exists in isolation, simple and pure
last_rejected.ruling: μοναχὸν can mean 'single/solitary'; 'single' conveys isolation adequately. Within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: through the paired quality, the power of each to mix with each comes forth
last_rejected.source_quote: διὰ τῆς συζύγου ποιότητος, ἡ δύναμις προέρχεται τοῦ ἀναμιχθῆναι ἑκάστῳ πρὸς ἕκαστον
last_rejected.why: The syntax is mangled; 'διὰ τῆς συζύγου ποιότητος' goes with 'ἀνακίρναται' below, not with 'προέρχται'; the power proceeds from the paired quality to mix, or the power to mix proceeds through the paired quality.
last_rejected.fix: through the paired quality the power proceeds for each to be mixed with each
last_rejected.ruling: διὰ τῆς συζύγου ποιότητος can modify προέρχεται; 'through paired quality power proceeds to mix' is defensible.

last_rejected.quote: by its dryness it returns again to fellowship with earth
last_rejected.source_quote: τῷ ξηρῷ δὲ πάλιν πρὸς τὴν κοινωνίαν τῆς γῆς ἐπανέρχεται
last_rejected.why: ἐπανέρχεται means 'returns' or 'goes back,' but the subject is fire's dryness, not fire itself; 'by its dryness it returns again to fellowship with earth' obscures that dryness is the means by which fire connects back to earth.
last_rejected.fix: and by its dryness it returns again to fellowship with earth
last_rejected.ruling: τῷ ξηρῷ as instrumental dative 'by its dryness' is correct; subject 'fire' is clear from context. Not obscured.
